raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old female patient was admitted to the emergency department. She had no history of trauma or medical surgery before her admittance to the hospital. She had complained of intermittent visual symptoms for 2 days, and no other symptoms were declared. She complained that she could hardly focus on details, especially when reading a book or watching television. The ocular movements were not affected, but the patient explained that objects seemed to be distorted for both eye evaluations. Her color vision was within normal limits in both eyes. Eye pupils were equally and bilaterally reactive to light. The fundoscopic examination was normal. The patient's general condition was evaluated as normal, conscious, and cooperative. Body temperature was 36.6 C, blood pressure was 107/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 97%. There was no power loss, and the Babinski test was negative in the physical examination. No tremor or dyskinesia was noted. The patient's total blood count, biochemistry, blood glucose level, and Brucella (Rose Bengal and immune capture with Coombs) tests indicated negative results. Anti-dsDNA antibodies, anti-Sjogren's Syndrome-related antigene A and B (anti-SSA and anti-SSB), antinuclear antibody (ANA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for cytomegalovirus (CMV), and perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA and c-ANCA) tests were all negative. However, the patient was found to be COVID-19 positive using the real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test. Before the patient received treatment at the clinic, the test was performed as part of a standard protocol. There were no cough, fever, chill, sore thought, or any other signs of viral infection.
The patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) since it was believed that she had a migraine with aura. The magnetic resonance (MR) images revealed a lesion located in the splenium of the CC, which was slightly hypointense on T1-weighted and frankly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence showed prominent hyperintense signals in the same location. The diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) indicated a diffusion restriction in the splenium, consistent with acute infarction. MR angiographic images showed that there was a discontinuity in the terminal branches of the right posterior cerebral artery (Figure 2). Doppler ultrasound imaging showed no atherosclerosis, thrombus, occlusion, or stenosis in the carotid arterial system and vertebral arteries. The patient has been put on acetylsalicylic acid therapy, and there was improvement in her follow-up examinations.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old previously healthy female presented with a 2-day history of intermittent bilateral visual distortion (metamorphopsia) and difficulty focusing on near details when reading or watching television.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 19-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with 2 days of intermittent visual disturbances characterized by distortion of objects in both eyes and inability to focus on fine print or television details, in the complete absence of fever or respiratory symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and surgical history; no history of trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-day bilateral visual distortion and difficulty focusing on details; negative for headache, fever, chills, cough, sore throat, motor weakness, or tremor.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and cooperative; temperature 36.6 C, blood pressure 107/62 mmHg, SpO2 97%. Intact extraocular movements, normal color vision, equal reactive pupils, and normal funduscopic examination; intact 5/5 limb motor strength, negative Babinski sign, and no tremor or dyskinesia.
objective.routine_investigations: Normal CBC, blood chemistry, and blood glucose; negative Brucella Rose Bengal and Coombs immunocapture tests; negative CMV PCR. Carotid and vertebral artery Doppler ultrasonography was normal. Standard screening nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 real-time RT-PCR test was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA were all negative. Brain MRI and MRA demonstrated an acute ischemic infarction in the splenium of the corpus callosum (T1 mildly hypointense, T2/FLAIR hyperintense, with restricted diffusion on DWI) accompanied by flow discontinuity in the terminal branches of the right posterior cerebral artery.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR and brain MRI/MRA demonstrating an acute diffusion-restricted infarction in the splenium of the corpus callosum with right distal posterior cerebral artery branch occlusion (and negative Brucella, CMV, autoimmune, and carotid/vertebral Doppler workups) confirmed asymptomatic COVID-19-associated acute ischemic stroke of the splenium of the corpus callosum presenting with isolated metamorphopsia. Treated with oral acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), resulting in clinical visual improvement on follow-up.
